result:
The kettle clicks off just as the light outside turns the color of old paper. I pour the water and watch the steam rise in loose spirals, each one briefly coherent before it disappears into the larger air of the room. There is no audience for this, no score being kept. The mug is chipped on one side; I always turn the chip away from my mouth without thinking, a small private courtesy between object and hand.

Outside, a single crow walks the fence line with the deliberate pace of someone who has already decided the day will be ordinary and is therefore free to notice everything. It stops, tilts its head at a discarded bottle cap, then continues. Nothing is resolved. The bottle cap remains exactly where it was. I find this restful.

Most of what we call meaning arrives the same way: not as a conclusion but as a slight rearrangement of attention. You notice the way afternoon light pools in the crease of a curtain and, for three seconds, the crease is the most precise fact in the world. Then the phone buzzes, or a car passes, and the crease returns to being fabric. The precision does not vanish; it simply stops being urgent. Urgency is optional. That is the part no one mentions when they talk about paying attention.

I take the first sip. The tea is too hot, which is correct. Waiting for it to cool would require a plan, and plans have a way of colonizing the minutes they were meant only to organize. Better to let the tongue negotiate its own treaty with temperature. The crow has reached the end of the fence and is now inspecting the sky as if the sky might contain a second, better fence. It does not. The crow shrugs in the way birds shrug—by simply ceasing to care—and drops into the neighbor’s yard.

Somewhere a radio is playing a song whose words I almost remember. The melody keeps offering the next note and then withholding it, the way memory does when it wants to stay interesting. I do not chase the lyric. Chasing would turn the almost-remembered into a task, and tasks accumulate dust. Instead I let the missing words hover just outside the edge of hearing, a small unfinished kindness the afternoon is willing to extend.

The light shifts another degree. The chip in the mug catches it and throws a tiny bright nick onto the table. For a moment the nick looks like a decision. Then it is only light again, and the decision, if there was one, has already been made by no one in particular: to stay here a little longer, doing nothing that needs to be finished.
